questions.question: How many OneLake instances does a Fabric tenant get?
choices: As many as the admin provisions, up to 100 per region
One per workspace, so each team gets an isolated lake
One per capacity, created automatically when each capacity is purchased in Azure
Exactly one, which can't be deleted and needs no provisioning
questions.explanation: Every Fabric tenant has a single OneLake: it can't be deleted, and you can't create more. Workspaces appear as containers and items as folders. One logical lake makes 'no copies' easy to promise, but it puts more weight on workspace, item and OneLake security design.

questions.question: In what open table formats does OneLake store and expose tables?
choices: CSV files with a separate JSON schema file per table
ORC only, converted to Delta when Spark reads it
Delta Parquet, with Iceberg supported through metadata virtualization
A proprietary columnar format that only Fabric engines can read, exported to Parquet on request
questions.explanation: OneLake stores tables as Delta Parquet and supports Iceberg via metadata virtualization (Iceberg tables can be written to or shortcut into OneLake). Open formats are the main reason Databricks and Fabric can share data without copying it.

questions.question: How can existing ADLS tools and SDKs access OneLake?
choices: OneLake supports ADLS Gen2 APIs; each workspace appears as a container and each item as a folder
Only through the Fabric REST API, which returns data as JSON pages
Only through a gateway that copies data into a customer-owned ADLS account
They can't. OneLake is reachable only through the Fabric portal and Power BI, so external tools need exports
questions.explanation: OneLake is built on ADLS and supports ADLS Gen2 APIs and SDKs, plus the OneLake file explorer for Windows. That compatibility is how external engines, including Azure Databricks, read and write OneLake data.

questions.question: What's the key difference between a Fabric Warehouse and a Lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint?
choices: The Warehouse stores data in a proprietary format, while the endpoint stores data as Delta Parquet
They're the same engine under two names; both accept identical T-SQL writes, but only the endpoint supports transactions
The endpoint supports DML through T-SQL, while the Warehouse only accepts data loaded by Spark notebooks
The Warehouse supports full T-SQL DDL and DML with multi-table transactions; the endpoint is read-only for data
questions.explanation: A Warehouse is developed with T-SQL and has full multi-table ACID transactions. A lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint can define views, functions and procedures and manage permissions, but can't modify data. Writes go through Spark or another engine. Customers coming from SQL Server often expect the endpoint to accept writes.

questions.question: A Spark job writes new rows to a lakehouse table, but a report on the SQL analytics endpoint doesn't show them for a while. Why?
choices: The endpoint only reads Delta checkpoints, which Fabric writes once per hour
The endpoint copies lakehouse data into a separate warehouse on a fixed 24-hour schedule, so new rows wait for that copy
Spark writes aren't visible to SQL until someone runs OPTIMIZE on the table manually
The endpoint relies on a background metadata sync that usually lags by under a minute, and can take longer
questions.explanation: The SQL analytics endpoint picks up lakehouse changes through a metadata sync. Microsoft says the lag is normally under a minute but can vary from seconds to minutes, and the background process stops after 15 minutes without query activity. 'New metadata sync' brings it to seconds, but existing endpoints must be upgraded. Many small files slow sync, so table maintenance matters.

questions.question: What does Microsoft say about the SQL analytics endpoint's sync when many lakehouses share one workspace?
choices: Sync is disabled automatically once a workspace holds more than ten lakehouses
Each lakehouse gets its own dedicated sync engine, so the number of lakehouses in a workspace never affects sync latency
Sync only runs for lakehouses that have a Warehouse defined in the same workspace
Sync runs as a single instance per workspace, so many lakehouses can increase latency and splitting workspaces may help
questions.explanation: Metadata sync is a single instance per workspace, so large numbers of lakehouses in one workspace can increase sync latency. Microsoft suggests splitting workspaces. Workspace design affects freshness as well as security.

questions.question: What is SQL database in Fabric?
choices: A Power BI semantic model that can be queried with T-SQL instead of DAX
A transactional database built on the Azure SQL Database engine, automatically replicated to OneLake as Parquet
A rebranded Synapse dedicated SQL pool with its own separate capacity billing
A read-only copy of a lakehouse exposed through a T-SQL endpoint, intended for reporting rather than operational apps
questions.explanation: SQL database in Fabric uses the same SQL Database engine as Azure SQL Database and is aimed at developers building operational apps. Data is replicated into OneLake automatically, and a SQL analytics endpoint is created, so operational data becomes analytics-ready without building pipelines. Usage draws on the Fabric capacity.

questions.question: In Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, what is an Eventhouse?
choices: A store optimized for time-based streaming events, queried with KQL
The alerting engine that triggers actions when conditions are met
A tenant-wide catalog of every stream available in the organization
A no-code tool for routing streams between sources and destinations with filters
questions.explanation: Eventhouse is the analytics store for time-based streaming events, organized by arrival time and queried with KQL (or T-SQL in a KQL queryset), with native anomaly detection. Eventstream moves and transforms streams, Activator triggers actions, and the Real-Time hub catalogs streams.

questions.question: Which Real-Time Intelligence component turns detected conditions into actions such as running a pipeline, a notebook or a Power Automate flow?
choices: KQL queryset
Eventstream
Activator
Real-Time hub
questions.explanation: Activator watches data and triggers actions (pipelines, Spark jobs, Dataflows, User Data Functions, Power Automate). It's the 'do something' piece. Microsoft also notes that 'real-time' data doesn't have to arrive at high rates and volumes.

questions.question: What does Eventstream do?
choices: Collects, transforms and routes real-time data to destinations without writing code
Stores years of raw event history for KQL analysis at the lowest possible storage cost
Runs Spark Structured Streaming jobs written in Scala or PySpark notebooks
Lists every stream in the tenant so users can discover and subscribe to them
questions.explanation: Eventstream is the no-code stream processor: filtering, windowed aggregations, dedupe and content-based routing to destinations like an Eventhouse or lakehouse. The Real-Time hub is the tenant-wide catalog of streams, including CDC, Event Hubs, IoT Hub and Fabric and Azure events.

questions.question: Which Data Factory item does Microsoft describe as the preferred solution for simplified data movement, supporting bulk, incremental and CDC copies?
choices: Apache Airflow job
Dataflow Gen2
Copy job
Notebook activity
questions.explanation: Copy job is Microsoft's preferred simple data-movement item (bulk, incremental and CDC). Pipelines orchestrate activities, Dataflow Gen2 handles low-code transformations, the copy activity gives manual control, and mirroring keeps a near real-time replica.

questions.question: What is Dataflow Gen2 used for in Fabric?
choices: Low-code data preparation and transformation (Power Query-style)
Replicating operational databases into OneLake in near real time
Scheduling Spark jobs across multiple workspaces with dependencies
Deploying items between dev, test and prod workspaces
questions.explanation: Dataflow Gen2 is the low-code transformation tool, with Microsoft citing over 300 transformations. It's familiar to Power BI users, but dataflows consume capacity, so heavy transformation logic is worth comparing against Spark or SQL on cost.

questions.question: What is the Native Execution Engine in Fabric Spark?
choices: A caching layer that stores query results in OneLake for repeated reports
A separate SQL engine that replaces Spark entirely for lakehouse queries once it's turned on, requiring notebook rewrites
A GPU runtime that requires rewriting notebooks in a Fabric-specific dialect
A vectorized engine (Velox via Apache Gluten) that runs supported Spark operators natively with no code changes
questions.explanation: The Native Execution Engine accelerates supported operators on Parquet, Delta and CSV and falls back to JVM Spark automatically for unsupported operators. It doesn't accelerate JSON, XML or Structured Streaming. Faster jobs mean fewer capacity units used, but Microsoft says actual results vary.

questions.question: What is a Fabric environment?
choices: A Git branch that holds a copy of the workspace's items for testing
A virtual network that isolates Spark clusters from the public internet
A workspace item that defines Spark session settings: runtime and compute, libraries and resources
A separate Fabric capacity reserved for development workloads, so testing never affects production users
questions.explanation: Environments bundle Spark compute settings, libraries and resources. Publishing in Full mode takes 3 to 6 minutes plus 1 to 3 minutes at session start, versus about 5 seconds in Quick mode. Library-heavy environments slow session starts, which users notice.

questions.question: What does Microsoft position Fabric Data Science for?
choices: Only for training large language models on GPU clusters in OneLake
Only for building Power BI reports with AI visuals on top of existing semantic models, without any model training
Building, deploying and operationalizing machine learning models, integrated with Azure Machine Learning
Only for running Copilot over notebooks without writing any code
questions.explanation: Fabric Data Science covers the ML lifecycle on OneLake data with notebooks and experiment tracking, integrated with Azure Machine Learning. Customers with mature ML on Databricks will compare model serving, feature management and governance depth, so be precise about which capabilities they actually need.

questions.question: What does Microsoft's Fabric overview describe Fabric IQ as unifying?
choices: Storage accounts across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud into one billing account, with a single invoice for all clouds
Git repositories and deployment pipelines across development teams
Capacity metrics from every workspace into one real-time throttling dashboard
Business semantics: ontology, planning, Fabric Graph, data agents, operations agents and semantic models
questions.explanation: Fabric IQ is Microsoft's business-semantics layer: ontologies, planning, Fabric Graph, data and operations agents, and semantic models. At Ignite 2026, Fabric IQ integrations in Microsoft Copilot were GA, while Fabric IQ in Excel and connectors for ChatGPT and Claude were in preview.

questions.question: Which Fabric capabilities did Microsoft announce as generally available at Ignite 2026?
choices: Native Unity Catalog hosting inside every Fabric workspace
Fabric apps (built with the open-source Rayfin SDK) and Database Hub
Fabric HorizonDB and the database agents for SQL and PostgreSQL in Database Hub
A new F0 SKU with unlimited free compute for development
questions.explanation: Per the Book of News, Fabric apps and Rayfin, and Database Hub in Fabric, are GA. Fabric HorizonDB (serverless PostgreSQL that pauses when idle) and SQL and PostgreSQL database agents are in preview. Fabric keeps expanding from analytics into operational apps.

questions.question: What is Fabric HorizonDB, announced in preview at Ignite 2026?
choices: A managed Unity Catalog metastore that Fabric hosts for Databricks customers
A Delta Lake replacement format optimized for time-series data in Eventhouse, replacing Parquet for streaming tables
A vector database for Copilot grounding that's billed in Copilot Credits
A serverless PostgreSQL database in Fabric that pauses when idle and replicates tables to OneLake
questions.explanation: Fabric HorizonDB is a serverless PostgreSQL offering in preview, positioned as a backend for Fabric apps, with tables replicated to OneLake. Azure HorizonDB reached GA separately, and mirroring Azure HorizonDB into Fabric is in preview. For customers, it widens Fabric's operational-database footprint.

questions.question: What underlies every Fabric workload?
choices: OneLake, the single logical data lake for the tenant
A separate ADLS account per experience
A Power BI Premium capacity per workload
Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pools, shared across workloads
questions.explanation: OneLake is the storage foundation under every workload: Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence, Data Science, Fabric IQ and industry solutions. Compute is paid through capacity, storage through OneLake.

questions.question: How do cross-database queries work in Fabric?
choices: Only Spark can join across items; T-SQL is limited to a single database per query
Data must first be copied into a single warehouse by a pipeline before any T-SQL query can join it to tables in other items
T-SQL can reference other warehouses, lakehouse endpoints and SQL databases by three-part name, with no data duplication
Cross-database queries require a linked server configured by a Fabric admin
questions.explanation: Fabric supports cross-database queries using three-part names (for example ContosoWarehouse.dbo.Sales) across warehouses and SQL analytics endpoints in the workspace, with zero data duplication. It's one of Fabric's practical strengths for SQL-centric teams.

questions.question: What availability SLA does Microsoft state for Fabric Data Factory activity runs?
choices: Runs start within one second of schedule 100% of the time
Runs start within one hour of their scheduled time 95% of the time, with no financial SLA
Runs start within four minutes of their scheduled time 99.9% of the time
There's no SLA for Data Factory in Fabric
questions.explanation: Microsoft states a 99.9% request SLA and that activity runs start within four minutes of schedule 99.9% of the time. That's relevant for tight batch windows and downstream SLAs.

questions.question: How can a team force a SQL analytics endpoint to pick up a data-only change to one table right away, once new metadata sync is on?
choices: Delete and recreate the lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint
Run VACUUM on the Delta table with a zero-hour retention
Run sys.sp_dw_refresh_ext_table for that table
Restart the Fabric capacity from the Azure portal
questions.explanation: With new metadata sync, sys.sp_dw_refresh_ext_table refreshes one table's data. For schema changes use the 'Refresh SQL analytics endpoint metadata' REST API or the portal's Refresh button. It's worth knowing when a customer complains about stale reports after a pipeline finishes.

questions.question: Which workloads does the Native Execution Engine not accelerate?
choices: Any workload on capacities smaller than F64
All SQL queries; it only accelerates PySpark DataFrame code
Any query that reads Delta tables, since the engine only accelerates plain Parquet and CSV
Structured Streaming, and JSON or XML processing, which fall back to JVM Spark
questions.explanation: The Native Execution Engine supports Parquet, Delta and CSV, and falls back to JVM Spark for unsupported operators, JSON, XML and Structured Streaming. Runtime 1.3 doesn't support ANSI mode with it, while Runtime 2.0 (Spark 4.1) does.

questions.question: What is Microsoft Fabric?
choices: Microsoft's resale of Azure Databricks under a new name, with Unity Catalog replaced by the Purview data catalog
An Azure networking service that connects Power BI to on-premises data sources through managed gateways and private endpoints
A per-user Power BI Premium add-on that adds Spark notebooks and pipelines to each licensed author's personal workspace
Microsoft's SaaS analytics platform that unifies data engineering, warehousing, real-time and Power BI on OneLake
questions.explanation: Fabric is a SaaS platform that puts data engineering (Spark), Data Factory, warehousing, databases, Real-Time Intelligence, data science, Power BI and Fabric IQ on one lake, OneLake. It's paid for with capacity rather than per workload. Power BI is now one part of it.

questions.question: What is OneLake?
choices: A separate data lake created for each workspace, so that every team gets its own isolated storage account
Fabric's single, tenant-wide data lake, built on ADLS, where tables are stored as Delta Parquet
A database engine that runs T-SQL queries over files, billed separately from the Fabric capacity it sits on
A Power BI cache that holds imported data for reports, refreshed on the schedule set by each semantic model
questions.explanation: OneLake is one data lake per tenant, built on ADLS. Every workspace is a container in it, and tables are stored as Delta Parquet, with Iceberg also supported. Storage is billed per GB, while reads and writes consume capacity CUs.

questions.question: What is KQL (Kusto Query Language) used for in Fabric?
choices: Defining measures and relationships in Power BI semantic models, in place of the older DAX language
Granting row-level and column-level permissions on lakehouse tables through OneLake security roles
Writing Spark transformations in notebooks when Python or Scala would be too slow for the job
Querying Eventhouse and KQL databases, built for fast analysis of time-series and log data
questions.explanation: KQL is the query language of Real-Time Intelligence's Eventhouse and KQL databases. It's designed for time-based events such as telemetry, logs and clickstreams. Measures in semantic models are still DAX, and lakehouse transformations are Spark or SQL.

questions.question: What does Activator do in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence?
choices: Activates trial capacity for new users so they can try Fabric features for free
Triggers actions, such as alerts or flows, when conditions in the data are met
Starts a paused Fabric capacity automatically whenever a user opens a report
Moves and transforms streaming data between sources without writing any code
questions.explanation: Activator watches data and takes an action when a condition is met, such as sending an alert or starting a flow. Moving and transforming streams without code is Eventstream's job, and Eventhouse stores the events for KQL queries. The Real-Time hub catalogs every stream in the tenant.

questions.question: What are Fabric apps, which reached GA at Ignite 2026?
choices: Apps built on Fabric with the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI, backed by stores such as SQL database
Third-party connectors sold through AppSource that add new data sources to Data Factory
Mobile versions of Fabric for iOS and Android that admins use to monitor capacity health while on the go
Power BI apps renamed, so that a published bundle of reports is now called a Fabric app
questions.explanation: Microsoft announced at Ignite 2026 that Fabric apps are GA: apps built on Fabric with the open-source Rayfin SDK and CLI, with backends such as SQL database or HorizonDB. It's part of Fabric's move from analytics into operational apps.

questions.question: What is Data Factory in Fabric?
choices: Fabric's catalog for finding, governing and securing data items
Fabric's data integration workload: pipelines, Dataflow Gen2, Copy job and mirroring
Fabric's database engine for transactional apps, built on Azure SQL
Fabric's machine learning workload for training, tracking and deploying models and experiments
questions.explanation: Data Factory covers data movement and orchestration: pipelines for orchestration, Dataflow Gen2 for low-code transformation, Copy job for simple bulk, incremental and CDC movement, and mirroring. The catalog for discovering and governing data is the OneLake catalog.

questions.question: A team is building an operational app and wants its transactional database to be available for analytics without building pipelines. Which Fabric item fits?
choices: A lakehouse with its SQL analytics endpoint
A Power BI semantic model in import mode
SQL database in Fabric
An Eventhouse with a KQL database
questions.explanation: SQL database in Fabric is an operational database on the Azure SQL Database engine. It runs on Fabric capacity and is replicated into OneLake automatically, so analytics can use the data without a pipeline. A lakehouse SQL endpoint is read-only, and Eventhouse is built for time-based events.

questions.question: A factory wants to analyze sensor readings within seconds and alert engineers when a machine runs hot. Which combination fits?
choices: A nightly pipeline into a lakehouse, an import-mode report, and an email subscription on the report
Eventstream to bring the data in, Eventhouse to query it with KQL, and Activator to send the alerts
Mirroring the sensor database into OneLake, then a Fabric data agent that users ask about temperatures
Dataflow Gen2 refreshed every hour into a warehouse, with Copilot in Power BI summarizing the results
questions.explanation: Real-Time Intelligence is built for this: Eventstream moves and transforms the stream without code, Eventhouse stores time-based events for fast KQL queries, and Activator triggers actions when a condition is met. Batch pipelines and hourly refreshes are too slow for seconds-level alerts.

questions.question: A team needs full T-SQL with inserts, updates and multi-table transactions over Delta tables in OneLake. Which Fabric item fits?
choices: A lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint
A KQL database in an Eventhouse
A Fabric Warehouse
A Power BI semantic model
questions.explanation: A Fabric Warehouse supports full T-SQL DDL and DML with multi-table transactions and stores its data as Delta in OneLake. A lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint is read-only; writes to a lakehouse go through Spark.

questions.question: A stakeholder says, 'Fabric is just Power BI Premium with a new name.' What's accurate?
choices: Fabric is a new database engine, unrelated to Power BI, that happens to share the same admin portal
Fabric replaced Power BI, which Microsoft retired when Fabric reached general availability
That's right: Fabric changed only the name and price of Power BI Premium and added no new workloads
Power BI is part of Fabric, but Fabric adds Spark, Data Factory, warehousing, databases and real-time on OneLake
questions.explanation: Fabric brings data engineering, Data Factory, warehousing, databases, Real-Time Intelligence, data science and Power BI together on OneLake. Power BI Premium P SKUs are being retired in favor of Fabric F SKUs, which is where the confusion comes from.

questions.question: How many capacity units (CUs) does an F64 provide?
choices: 64 CUs
128 CUs
640 CUs
6.4 CUs
questions.explanation: The number in an F SKU is its CU count: F2 = 2 CUs up to F2048 = 2,048 CUs. Microsoft's table now runs up to F8192. A useful anchor for Spark: 1 CU = 2 Spark vCores, so an F64 has 128 vCores before bursting.

questions.question: Which F SKU does Microsoft's licensing table list alongside Power BI Premium P1?
questions.explanation: The table lines up P1 with F64, P2 with F128 and P3 with F256, and so on. Microsoft cautions that it isn't a statement of functional or licensing equivalence. F64 matters because it's the threshold at which free users can view Power BI content.

questions.question: What's Microsoft's position on Power BI Premium per-capacity (P) SKUs?
choices: They're being retired; new and existing customers should consider Fabric F SKUs instead
They're required for any Fabric workload other than Power BI
They're the recommended path for all new customers through 2030, with F SKUs reserved for Spark-only workloads
They're being repriced to match F SKUs but remain fully available to everyone
questions.explanation: Microsoft is consolidating purchase options and retiring P SKUs. P SKUs remain only for customers with them on an active Enterprise Agreement. F SKUs are Azure resources: billed per second with a one-minute minimum, pausable, reservation- and MACC-eligible.

questions.question: On an F32 capacity, what do report consumers need to view Power BI content shared in a workspace?
choices: Nothing. Any Fabric capacity of any size lets free users view shared Power BI content
A Pro or PPU license (or an individual trial); free users can't view it below F64
A Fabric capacity admin role assigned to each consumer
A Copilot license, since F32 routes reports through Copilot
questions.explanation: Below F64, viewing Power BI content outside My workspace needs Pro, PPU or an individual trial. At F64 and above, free users with a viewer role can view content. Many small-capacity Fabric business cases miss this: an F32 plus 2,000 Pro viewers can cost far more than expected.

questions.question: What are the US list prices for Power BI Pro and Premium Per User (PPU), paid yearly?
choices: $10 and $20 per user per month
$14 and $30 per user per month
$20 and $40 per user per month
$14 and $24 per user per month
questions.explanation: Microsoft's pricing page lists Pro at $14 and PPU at $24 per user per month, paid yearly. They rose from $10 and $20 in April 2025. Older business cases often still use the old figures.

questions.question: A customer buys PPU for its analysts and assumes it can now build lakehouses and notebooks. What's wrong?
choices: PPU allows lakehouses but not notebooks or warehouses
PPU doesn't provision a Fabric capacity; non-Power BI items still need an F or trial capacity
PPU only works with P SKUs, so they must buy a P1 first
Nothing. PPU includes an F8 capacity for each licensed user, which covers lakehouses and notebooks
questions.explanation: Microsoft is explicit that PPU doesn't provision a Fabric capacity. PPU adds Premium Power BI features (48 refreshes a day, models over 1 GB, XMLA) for licensed users, and Microsoft says it's more cost-effective for fewer than 250 users. Fabric items like lakehouses, warehouses and notebooks need F capacity.

questions.question: According to Microsoft, below roughly how many users is PPU usually more cost-effective than capacity for Premium Power BI features?
choices: Fewer than 250 users
Fewer than 2,500 users
Fewer than 25 users
Fewer than 10,000 users
questions.explanation: Microsoft's license guide says PPU is more cost-effective for fewer than 250 users. The real comparison also has to include viewers: at F64+ free users can view, which changes the math for broad audiences.

questions.question: What limits apply to semantic models in a Pro (shared capacity) workspace?
choices: No size limit and unlimited refreshes
10 GB model size and 48 scheduled refreshes a day
100 MB model size and one refresh a day
1 GB model size and 8 scheduled refreshes a day
questions.explanation: Pro workspaces cap models at 1 GB with 8 refreshes a day and 10 GB storage per user. PPU allows models over 1 GB, 48 refreshes a day and the XMLA endpoint. These limits often push customers toward capacity, and toward Fabric.

questions.question: How does Azure bill Fabric capacity on pay-as-you-go?
choices: Per month, with no proration
Per day, regardless of usage
Per second, with a one-minute minimum
Per full hour, rounded up to the next whole hour
questions.explanation: Fabric capacities bill per second with a one-minute minimum. That's what makes pause-and-resume and scale-up-for-a-window strategies worthwhile on pay-as-you-go capacity.

questions.question: How is a Fabric capacity reservation discount applied?
choices: To OneLake storage only, while compute stays at pay-as-you-go
To the whole Azure bill, including non-Fabric services
As a lump-sum credit at the start of each month, applied regardless of whether the capacity is used
To capacity units on an hourly basis; storage and networking stay at pay-as-you-go rates
questions.explanation: Reservation discounts apply to CUs hourly. Microsoft's reservation page notes storage and networking aren't covered. If a reserved capacity sits idle or paused for an hour, that hour's benefit is lost. Microsoft's pricing page cites savings of around 41% versus pay-as-you-go.

questions.question: How are Fabric capacity overages priced?
choices: At the reservation rate, because the capacity is already reserved and overage is treated as extra reserved CUs
Free up to 10% above the purchased CU level
At half the pay-as-you-go rate to encourage bursting
At pay-as-you-go rates, even on a reserved capacity; reservation discounts don't apply
questions.explanation: The Azure pricing page says overage can apply to pay-as-you-go or reserved capacities but is priced at the pay-as-you-go rate and isn't eligible for reservation discounts. Overage is on by default, admins can set a 24-hour limit, and checks run every 5 minutes, so billing can exceed the limit.

questions.question: An admin sets a 24-hour limit on paid overages. Why can billed overage still exceed it?
choices: The limit resets every hour, so it never actually caps a day
Overages are checked every 5 minutes, so usage can pass the limit before enforcement
The limit applies only to background operations, so interactive overage is never counted toward it
Reserved capacities ignore overage limits entirely
questions.explanation: The Azure pricing page notes overage checks run every 5 minutes, so billing can exceed the configured limit. Treat it as a guardrail, not a hard ceiling, the same lesson as many Copilot spend controls.

questions.question: What happens financially when an admin pauses a Fabric capacity that has accumulated smoothed usage and overages?
choices: The accumulated usage is forgiven, which is why pausing to escape throttling also saves money
It's converted into OneLake storage credit
It's carried over and charged when the capacity next resumes
The remaining smoothed usage and overages are summed and added to the Azure bill at pause time
questions.explanation: Pausing bills the outstanding smoothed and overage usage immediately. It also clears throttling and returns the capacity to a healthy state. 'Pause to escape throttling' works, but it isn't free.

questions.question: Who can pause or resume a Fabric F SKU?
choices: Only Microsoft support, through a service request
Only the Fabric administrator, from the admin portal's capacity settings page in Fabric
Anyone holding the Azure RBAC suspend and resume actions on the capacity resource
Any workspace admin whose workspace sits on the capacity
questions.explanation: F SKUs are Azure resources, so pause and resume are Azure RBAC actions (read, write, suspend, resume). Microsoft recommends a custom role rather than broad built-in ones. Pausing makes content on the capacity unavailable, so automation needs care.

questions.question: Which capabilities are not available on a Fabric trial capacity?
choices: Copilot and AI experiences (data agents, AI functions), Private Link and free mirroring storage
Lakehouses, notebooks and warehouses, which require paid capacity because they store data in OneLake
Warehouses and pipelines
Power BI reports and dashboards
questions.explanation: Trials last 60 days and don't support Copilot, AI experiences, Trusted Workspace Access, Private Link, autoscale or free mirroring storage. When a trial expires, items go inactive and data is kept for 7 days. Proofs of concept for AI features need paid capacity.

questions.question: How long does a Fabric trial capacity last?
choices: 14 days
180 days
60 days
30 days
questions.explanation: A Fabric trial runs 60 days, and changing its size doesn't extend it. Microsoft describes trial capacities as F4 or F64 in size, with up to 1 TB of OneLake storage. Plan proofs of concept to finish inside that window or budget for paid capacity.

questions.question: How much free mirroring storage comes with an F64?
choices: 64 TB: one free terabyte per capacity unit
None; mirrored data is billed like any other storage
Unlimited, as long as the source is Azure SQL
1 TB per capacity, regardless of size
questions.explanation: Fabric includes 1 TB of free mirroring storage per CU purchased (F2 gives 2 TB, F64 gives 64 TB). Replication compute is free. Querying the mirrored data consumes CUs normally. Trials don't get free mirroring storage.

questions.question: What does Microsoft's pricing page say about 'Fabric zero-provisioned (F0)'?
choices: It's a reserved SKU that requires a three-year commitment
It's the new name for the 60-day trial capacity
It includes on-demand billing by default, so usage is billed as consumed without a provisioned CU size
It's a free capacity that never incurs compute charges, intended for development and learning workloads
questions.explanation: F0 is listed on the Azure pricing page as including on-demand billing by default, and OneLake documents on-demand billing for F0 and paid capacities. On-demand and Spark on-demand usage bills at regional pay-as-you-go CU-hour rates, and reservation discounts don't apply. Some features, such as surge protection, don't work on F0.

questions.question: When on-demand billing for Apache Spark is enabled on a capacity, what changes?
choices: Spark jobs stop consuming the capacity's CUs and bill separately, without bursting or falling back to capacity
Spark jobs get 3x burst automatically, at no extra cost
Spark jobs run free as long as the capacity is reserved
Spark jobs keep using the capacity first and switch to on-demand billing only when the capacity is being throttled
questions.explanation: With on-demand Spark, jobs no longer consume capacity CUs and are billed pay-as-you-go. The admin sets a max CU limit that governs concurrency. It doesn't burst from or fall back to capacity, and reservation discounts don't apply. This isolates Spark spikes from Power BI, but it's a separate meter to budget.

questions.question: Which of these is a prerequisite for buying a Fabric capacity?
choices: An Azure subscription with the Microsoft.Fabric resource provider registered and enough CU quota
A Microsoft 365 E5 license for the purchaser and an existing Power BI Premium P SKU in the tenant
A Power BI Pro license for every user who will read data on the capacity
An existing Azure Databricks workspace in the same region
questions.explanation: Buying Fabric capacity needs an Azure subscription, a Free or Power BI license, the Microsoft.Fabric resource provider registered, and CU quota. B2B guest users can't be capacity admins, which affects partner-managed setups.

questions.question: Is Fabric capacity spend eligible to count toward a Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC)?
choices: Yes. Microsoft's pricing page says Fabric is MACC-eligible
No, because Fabric is billed as a Microsoft 365 product, not Azure
Only P SKUs count toward MACC
Only Fabric reservations count, not pay-as-you-go
questions.explanation: Fabric F SKUs are Azure resources and MACC-eligible, as are Azure Databricks and Copilot Credits bought PAYG or P3. MACC usually isn't a tiebreaker between Fabric and Databricks on Azure: both burn down the same commitment.

questions.question: For 'embed for your organization' on an F16 capacity, what do end users need?
choices: Nothing, because embedding bypasses per-user licensing
A Pro or PPU license each (or an individual trial)
A Microsoft 365 Copilot license
A Fabric capacity admin role
questions.explanation: Embedding for your organization on F SKUs below F64 (and on all A SKUs) requires each user to have Pro, PPU or a trial. At F64+ or on P capacities, free users can view. 'App owns data' embedding for external customers needs no end-user license.

questions.question: What can Power BI A SKUs and EM SKUs run?
choices: Everything an F SKU can, plus Copilot
All Fabric workloads including Spark and Warehouse, at a lower price than the equivalent F SKUs
Spark and Warehouse, but not Power BI
Only Power BI items (A SKUs); EM SKUs don't support Fabric workloads either
questions.explanation: EM SKUs don't support Fabric, and A SKUs support only Power BI items. Customers on embedded SKUs who want lakehouses or warehouses need F capacity.

questions.question: Is OneLake storage included in the capacity price?
choices: Yes, but only on reserved capacities
Yes. Each CU includes 1 TB of OneLake storage for any kind of data, not just mirroring
No. Storage is billed in CUs at 1 CU per GB
No. Storage is billed separately per GB per month and doesn't consume CUs
questions.explanation: OneLake storage is billed pay-as-you-go per GB and doesn't consume CUs. Reads and writes do consume CUs. The 1 TB per CU free allowance applies only to mirroring storage. A Fabric TCO needs separate compute, storage and transaction lines, like any lakehouse.

questions.question: Is storage in a deleted Fabric workspace still billed?
choices: Only for mirrored data, not lakehouse data
Only if the workspace was on a reserved capacity
No. Deleting a workspace stops all billing immediately, including for any data it contained
Yes, during the deleted-workspace retention period, which is configurable from 7 to 90 days
questions.explanation: The pricing page notes storage in deleted workspaces is billed during retention (7 to 90 days, configurable). Soft-deleted files are also billed at the active rate. Cleanups don't reduce cost until retention ends.

questions.question: What is a Fabric capacity?
choices: A limit on how many reports a workspace can publish before it has to be upgraded
The pool of compute, sized in capacity units, that a tenant's Fabric workloads run on
A per-user license that decides which Fabric workloads and items a person is allowed to open
A storage quota in OneLake that sets how many terabytes each workspace may keep
questions.explanation: A capacity is the compute pool behind Fabric workloads, sized in capacity units (an F64 has 64 CUs). It's billed per second pay-as-you-go or reserved, and it's MACC-eligible. OneLake storage is billed separately, per GB.

questions.question: What's the difference between a Fabric F SKU and Power BI Premium Per User (PPU)?
choices: An F SKU is a per-user license for Fabric workloads; PPU is shared compute for all of a tenant's Power BI reports
They're the same thing priced two ways: PPU is simply the monthly-billed version of an F64 capacity
An F SKU covers Power BI only; PPU covers Spark, pipelines, warehouses and every other Fabric workload
An F SKU is shared compute for all Fabric workloads; PPU is a per-user license for premium Power BI features
questions.explanation: An F SKU provisions capacity units that every Fabric workload in its workspaces shares. PPU ($24 per user per month) adds premium Power BI features such as larger models, 48 refreshes a day and XMLA for the people who hold it, and it doesn't provision Fabric capacity.

questions.question: A customer says, 'We bought Fabric, so Power BI is included for everyone.' What's accurate?
choices: Free users can view content only on F64 or larger; below that viewers need Pro or PPU, and authors always do
That's right: any F SKU lets every user in the tenant both view and publish reports without a Power BI license
Fabric replaces Power BI entirely, so reports must be rebuilt as Fabric apps before anyone can view them
Viewers are free on any capacity, but authors need an F64 of their own to publish their reports
questions.explanation: On capacities below F64, people viewing Power BI content need Pro or PPU. At F64 and above, free users with a viewer role can view. Building and sharing content needs Pro ($14) or PPU ($24) at any size. Small-capacity business cases often miss the viewer licenses.

questions.question: A CFO says, 'We reserved our Fabric capacity, so our bill is fixed.' What's accurate?
choices: It discounts capacity units only; storage, networking and other usage bill at pay-as-you-go rates
Reservations fix the bill, but only in months when the capacity is never paused or scaled
That's right: a reservation covers capacity, OneLake storage and networking at one fixed monthly price
Reservations fix the bill only for F64 and larger; smaller capacities are always billed by the second
questions.explanation: A Fabric reservation applies its discount hourly to capacity units. Storage and networking aren't covered, and an hour when the reserved capacity sits idle or paused loses that hour's benefit. Budget storage separately, and watch usage that bills outside the reservation.

questions.question: A team has 2,000 report viewers and 20 authors. Ignoring the capacity's own price, how much Power BI Pro licensing ($14 per user per month) does each option need?
choices: About $28,280 a month on either size of capacity
Nothing on either, because Fabric capacity includes Pro
On an F32, about $28,280 a month; on an F64, about $280
On an F32, about $280 a month; on an F64, about $28,280
questions.explanation: Below F64, viewers need Pro, so an F32 means 2,020 × $14 = $28,280 a month. At F64, free users can view, so only the 20 authors need Pro: 20 × $14 = $280. For broad audiences, the jump to F64 can pay for itself.

questions.question: Over what window does Fabric smooth background operations such as scheduled refreshes and pipelines?
choices: 1 hour
24 hours
7 days
5 minutes
questions.explanation: Background operations are smoothed over 24 hours. Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes, depending on how many CUs they use. Smoothing lets a small capacity run big jobs, but it also means a heavy nightly batch keeps 'costing' capacity for the next day.

questions.question: How are interactive operations, such as a report query, smoothed?
choices: Over at least 5 minutes, and up to 64 minutes for heavier operations
Over exactly 24 hours, the same window that's used for background jobs
They aren't smoothed; they're charged in the 30 seconds they run
Over 7 days, to avoid throttling during the business week
questions.explanation: Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes, up to 64 minutes depending on CU usage. Fabric evaluates capacity in 30-second timepoints (2,880 per day). Ambiguous operations are classed as background.

questions.question: What is bursting in Fabric capacity?
choices: Automatically buying the next bigger SKU when demand spikes, then scaling back down overnight
Operations temporarily using more compute than the SKU provides, paid back through smoothing
Running Spark jobs on GPUs for faster results
Moving workloads to another region during peak hours
questions.explanation: Bursting lets operations temporarily use more compute than provisioned, so smaller capacities can run larger jobs, and smoothing spreads the cost over time. Bursting and smoothing don't apply to Spark when on-demand Spark billing is enabled.

questions.question: What does Fabric's 'overage protection' stage allow before any throttling starts?
choices: Interactive jobs are delayed by 10 seconds
Jobs can use up to 10 minutes of future capacity without throttling
Jobs can exceed capacity by 10% indefinitely
Jobs can use up to 24 hours of future capacity before anything is throttled
questions.explanation: Stages by future capacity consumed: up to 10 minutes is overage protection (no throttling); 10 to 60 minutes delays new interactive jobs by 20 seconds; 60 minutes to 24 hours rejects new interactive jobs; beyond 24 hours, all new requests are rejected.

questions.question: A capacity has used 30 minutes of future capacity. What do report users experience?
choices: New interactive requests are delayed by 20 seconds at submission
All interactive requests are rejected with a CapacityLimitExceeded error
Nothing. Throttling only starts after 24 hours
Background jobs are cancelled mid-run
questions.explanation: Between 10 and 60 minutes of future usage, Fabric delays new interactive jobs by 20 seconds. Users notice slow reports first, well before errors appear, which is why 'Power BI is slow' tickets often trace back to someone's heavy Spark or dataflow job on the same capacity.

questions.question: At what level of future capacity use does Fabric start rejecting all new requests, background jobs included?
choices: More than 7 days
More than 10 minutes
More than 60 minutes
More than 24 hours
questions.explanation: Interactive rejection starts at 60 minutes. Background rejection, which rejects all new requests, starts beyond 24 hours. Users see errors like 'Your organization's Fabric compute capacity has exceeded its limits.' At that stage scheduled pipelines fail too, which can break downstream SLAs.

questions.question: When throttling begins, what happens to operations already running?
choices: They run to completion; throttling applies only to new requests
They're paused until carryforward is paid down
They're moved to another capacity automatically
They're cancelled immediately and must be resubmitted by the user who started them
questions.explanation: Throttling applies only to requests submitted after it starts, and in-flight operations finish. One very large job can therefore push a capacity deep into debt before anything stops it. Surge protection exists to cut that off earlier.

questions.question: How does a throttled capacity recover?
choices: Unused capacity in each timepoint burns down the carryforward until the overage is paid off
Carryforward is billed to the customer and throttling ends instantly
Microsoft forgives all outstanding carryforward at midnight UTC each day, so throttling ends then
Recovery requires a support ticket to reset the capacity
questions.explanation: Usage beyond the 10-minute window becomes carryforward, and each timepoint's unused CUs burn it down. Throttling continues until it's paid off. Scaling up burns it down faster but doesn't clear it instantly, while pausing clears it by billing the accumulated amount at once.

questions.question: A capacity is deep in throttling before a board meeting. Which option immediately returns it to a healthy state?
choices: Turning on surge protection, which forgives existing debt
Pausing and resuming it, which bills the accumulated future usage at pause time
Moving the reports to a Pro workspace, which resets the capacity
Scaling up by one SKU, which erases all existing carryforward the moment the new size applies
questions.explanation: Pausing bills the accumulated smoothed and overage usage, and a resumed capacity starts with zero future usage. Scaling up only burns down debt faster, and surge protection prevents future debt rather than clearing existing debt. It's an emergency lever with a cost.

questions.question: The Capacity Metrics app shows utilization above 100%. Does that mean the capacity is throttled?
choices: No. Utilization can never exceed 100% in Fabric
Not necessarily. Check the Throttling chart, because bursting and smoothing allow utilization above 100%
Yes. Anything above 100% means every request is being rejected until utilization drops back under 100%
Yes, and Microsoft automatically bills an upgrade to the next SKU
questions.explanation: Microsoft notes utilization above 100% doesn't automatically mean throttling, because of bursting and smoothing. The Throttling chart shows the real state. Misreading this leads customers to over-buy capacity.

questions.question: What does capacity-level surge protection do?
choices: Automatically scales the capacity up to the next SKU during spikes and back down when usage returns to normal
Refunds overage charges caused by unexpected spikes
Blocks interactive Power BI queries so background jobs can finish
Rejects new background operations when 24-hour background usage passes a threshold, until it recovers
questions.explanation: Capacity-level surge protection sets a background rejection threshold and a recovery threshold against the 24-hour background percentage. It protects interactive users from runaway background jobs. Microsoft notes the threshold isn't an upper limit, and in-progress jobs aren't stopped.

questions.question: What does workspace-level surge protection let an admin do?
choices: Cap a workspace's CU use over a rolling 24 hours and block it, with a 'Mission critical' exemption option
Move a workspace automatically to a larger capacity when it spikes
Assign each workspace its own dedicated capacity at no extra cost, so busy workspaces never affect each other
Guarantee each workspace a fixed number of Spark nodes
questions.explanation: Workspace surge protection caps CU use as a percentage of capacity on a rolling 24-hour window (5% of an F2 is 2.4 CU hours a day). Workspaces can be Available, Mission critical or Blocked. Checks run every five minutes, so Microsoft calls these soft limits, and autoscale compute is excluded.

questions.question: Does marking a workspace 'Mission critical' exempt it from capacity-level surge protection?
choices: Yes, but only for interactive Power BI operations
Mission critical only changes the workspace's color in the portal
Yes. Mission-critical workspaces are never rejected by any surge protection setting at any level
No. Mission critical exempts it from workspace limits only, not capacity-level surge protection
questions.explanation: Microsoft states 'Mission critical' doesn't override capacity-level surge protection. Surge protection works only on provisioned Fabric SKUs, not F0. Critical workloads may still need their own capacity.

questions.question: How many Spark vCores does one Fabric capacity unit provide?
choices: 8 vCores per CU, so an F64 has 512 vCores
Spark doesn't use CUs; it's always billed separately
2 vCores per CU, so an F64 has 128 vCores before bursting
1 vCore per CU, so an F64 has 64 Spark vCores before bursting
questions.explanation: One CU equals two Spark vCores, so an F64 has 128. With the 3x burst multiplier that's 384 vCores for concurrent Spark work. Bursting is borrowed capacity that's paid back through smoothing.

questions.question: What burst multiplier does Fabric apply to Spark vCores?
choices: 3x
2x
No burst for Spark
questions.explanation: Spark gets a 3x burst multiplier, so an F64's 128 vCores can burst to 384. Starter pools start in about 5 to 10 seconds on Medium nodes, but Microsoft notes their availability isn't guaranteed.

questions.question: How quickly does usage data appear in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, and can it send alerts?
choices: Instantly, and it includes built-in email alerts at 80% and 100% utilization that capacity admins can't turn off
Within about 10 to 15 minutes, and it doesn't support alerts; use Real-Time hub capacity events for that
Weekly, with alerts sent to the Fabric admin by default
Once a day, with alerts configured in Azure Monitor
questions.explanation: The Metrics app shows usage after 10 to 15 minutes and keeps a 14-day view, but it doesn't alert. Microsoft points to Fabric capacity overview events in the Real-Time hub for capacity alerts. Customers should set alerts up, or they'll learn about throttling from users.

questions.question: How many CU-seconds does an F64 have in each 30-second timepoint?
choices: 3,840 (64 CUs × 60 seconds per minute)
1,920 (64 CUs × 30 seconds)
questions.explanation: Capacity per timepoint is CUs × 30 seconds, so 1,920 CU-seconds for an F64. Microsoft also offers a Fabric SKU Estimator (preview) for sizing. Real usage from a pilot beats any estimate.

questions.question: Are Real-Time Intelligence operations subject to the 20-second interactive delay stage?
choices: No. Microsoft notes Real-Time Intelligence isn't subject to that delay stage
Yes, and the delay is longer, at 60 seconds
Only Eventstream is delayed, never Eventhouse
Yes. Every workload, including Eventhouse and Eventstream, gets the same delay
questions.explanation: The throttling page notes Real-Time Intelligence isn't subject to the 20-second delay. Throttling behavior varies by workload. Warehouse operations are almost all classed as background.

questions.question: What error status do users see when Fabric rejects requests because of capacity limits?
choices: ThrottledByAzure, which only workspace admins can see
CapacityLimitExceeded, with messages such as 'Cannot load model due to reaching capacity limits'
QuotaExceeded, which disappears after the user signs out
HTTP 402 Payment Required, with a link that lets the user buy more capacity directly in the Azure portal
questions.explanation: Rejected requests return CapacityLimitExceeded with messages like 'Your organization's Fabric compute capacity has exceeded its limits. Try again later.' Rejected operations show only minimal detail in the Metrics app because they never started. It helps to recognize these errors on a support call.

questions.question: A customer's finance dashboards slow down every morning after a large overnight Spark load on the same F64. Which approach does Fabric support for isolating them?
choices: Set Power BI to 'priority mode', which lets interactive queries ignore capacity limits during business hours
Nothing. All workloads in a tenant share one global pool
Move Spark to on-demand billing or a separate capacity, and use surge protection to cap background use
Convert the dashboards to Direct Lake, which uses no CUs
questions.explanation: Capacities are the isolation boundary. On-demand Spark takes Spark off the capacity, surge protection limits background usage, and separate capacities isolate workloads fully. Direct Lake still consumes CUs. A 24-hour smoothed overnight load keeps eating the next day's interactive headroom.

questions.question: How many days of history does the Capacity Metrics app's compute page show?
choices: 90 days
13 months
14 days
24 hours
questions.explanation: The compute page covers 14 days. For longer trend analysis and chargeback, export the data or use workspace monitoring and observability features. Microsoft previewed broader Fabric observability in 2026.

questions.question: What is carryforward in Fabric capacity management?
choices: Unused capacity units from one month that roll over into the next month's invoice as a credit against future usage
The capacity debt that builds up when usage exceeds what smoothing can absorb, paid down by later unused capacity
A reservation feature that moves unused reserved hours to another capacity in the same Azure subscription
The setting that copies a capacity's workspaces into its Azure-paired region for disaster recovery
questions.explanation: When usage runs ahead of what smoothing can absorb, the excess becomes carryforward. Unused CUs in later 30-second timepoints pay it down, and throttling continues until it's paid off. Pausing the capacity bills the accumulated amount at once and resets it.

questions.question: What is the Fabric Capacity Metrics app for?
choices: Monitoring capacity usage and throttling over the last 14 days
Sending alerts to admins as soon as throttling starts
Setting a capacity's size and pausing it on a schedule
Billing each workspace for the capacity units it consumed
questions.explanation: The Capacity Metrics app is a Power BI app for watching capacity use and throttling over 14 days, with about 10 to 15 minutes of delay. It can't send alerts, so use Real-Time hub capacity events for that. Sizing and pausing happen in the Azure portal.

questions.question: What's the difference between throttling and surge protection in Fabric?
choices: Throttling is a setting an admin turns on; surge protection is what Fabric does automatically once a capacity is overused
Throttling is automatic when a capacity is overused; surge protection is an admin limit that rejects jobs early
They're the same mechanism: surge protection is the name of the final throttling stage, after 24 hours of overuse
Throttling applies only to Spark jobs; surge protection applies only to Power BI reports and semantic model queries
questions.explanation: Throttling happens automatically when a capacity has used too much future capacity: delays, then rejections. Surge protection is something an admin configures to reject new background operations once a capacity, or a single workspace, passes a threshold, protecting interactive users before throttling sets in. Its checks run every five minutes, so its limits are soft.

questions.question: A heavy overnight job finished at 3 a.m., yet the capacity is still near its limit at noon. Why?
choices: The job is still running in the background, because Fabric never stops finished jobs
Fabric bills the job again every hour until a capacity admin manually clears it
Interactive users are being charged for the job until they close their reports
Background jobs are smoothed over 24 hours, so the job keeps using capacity long after it ends
questions.explanation: Fabric spreads background operations over 24 hours. That lets a small capacity run big jobs, but a heavy nightly batch keeps taking a share of capacity through the next day. Schedule heavy work with that in mind, or isolate it with on-demand Spark, surge protection or a separate capacity.

questions.question: A customer on a zero-provisioned F0 capacity wants surge protection. What's the catch?
choices: Surge protection on F0 must be requested from Microsoft support
Surge protection needs provisioned capacity, so it doesn't work on F0
Surge protection costs an extra 10% of the capacity's price on F0
Surge protection on F0 protects background jobs and blocks interactive ones
questions.explanation: F0 has no provisioned compute and bills usage on demand, and some features, surge protection among them, need provisioned capacity. Customers who want to protect interactive users from runaway jobs need a provisioned F SKU.

questions.question: A nightly background job uses 1,000,000 CU-seconds on an F8. After 24-hour smoothing, roughly what share of the capacity's day does it take?
choices: About 50%, half of the day's capacity
About 145%, more than the whole day's capacity
About 1.4%, too little to notice
About 14%, leaving plenty of headroom
questions.explanation: An F8 provides 8 × 86,400 = 691,200 CU-seconds a day. 1,000,000 ÷ 691,200 is about 1.45, so the job alone needs about 145% of a day's capacity, which builds carryforward and throttling. Move the job to on-demand Spark, size up, or split it.

questions.question: What is a OneLake shortcut?
choices: A saved SQL query that materializes results as a new Delta table
A scheduled copy job that duplicates external data into OneLake each night so engines can read it locally
A pointer, like a symbolic link, that makes data in another location appear in OneLake without copying it
A bookmark in the Fabric portal that opens a storage account in Azure
questions.explanation: Shortcuts behave like symbolic links: deleting a shortcut leaves the target alone, but moving or deleting the target breaks it. They're created in lakehouses and KQL databases and are readable by Spark, SQL analytics endpoints (Tables), KQL and Direct Lake.

questions.question: Which external storage can OneLake shortcuts point to?
choices: Only ADLS Gen2 accounts in the same Azure region as the capacity; other clouds and SaaS sources need mirroring or pipelines instead
Only Amazon S3, since Azure storage must use pipelines instead
Only other Fabric items; external storage requires mirroring
ADLS Gen2, Azure Blob, Amazon S3 and S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage, Dataverse, Iceberg, OneDrive and SharePoint
questions.explanation: External shortcut targets include ADLS Gen2, Blob, S3 and S3-compatible storage, GCS, Dataverse, Iceberg, and OneDrive and SharePoint. On-premises sources go through the on-premises data gateway. Internal targets include lakehouses, warehouses, mirrored databases and mirrored Azure Databricks catalogs.

questions.question: Whose identity does OneLake use to authorize reads through an internal shortcut (one Fabric item to another)?
choices: The workspace identity of the workspace that holds the target
A Fabric system account that bypasses item permissions
The calling user's identity, so the caller needs permission on the target
The shortcut creator's identity, used for everyone who reads through the shortcut
questions.explanation: For internal shortcuts, OneLake uses the calling user's identity. One exception: Direct Lake over SQL and T-SQL in Delegated identity mode pass the calling item owner's identity. Microsoft recommends Direct Lake on OneLake, or T-SQL in User identity mode, to avoid this.

questions.question: How do ADLS and S3 shortcuts authorize access to external storage?
choices: Through the Fabric admin's personal credentials, set once per tenant
Anonymous access, so the external storage must be made public
Through cloud connections bound to the shortcut, rather than each reader's own credentials
Each reader's own Entra ID token is forwarded to S3 or ADLS, so external storage checks every user
questions.explanation: Microsoft says ADLS and S3 shortcuts delegate authorization through cloud connections, and binding one requires permission on that connection. Everyone reading through the shortcut effectively uses the connection's access to the external store, so pair it with OneLake security on the Fabric side.

questions.question: Why does OneLake offer shortcut caching, and for which sources?
choices: To cut cross-cloud egress costs, for GCS, S3, S3-compatible and on-premises gateway shortcuts
To create a permanent copy so the source can be deleted safely
To bypass the source system's security for faster reads
To speed up ADLS Gen2 shortcuts in the same region, by keeping a permanent local copy of every file
questions.explanation: Shortcut caching reduces egress costs for cross-cloud access. It's supported for GCS, S3, S3-compatible and on-premises gateway shortcuts, with retention of 1 to 28 days that resets on each access, and files over 1 GB aren't cached. It's enabled per workspace under Workspace settings > OneLake.

questions.question: Workspace A (capacity 1) has a shortcut to data stored in workspace B (capacity 2). Users query through the shortcut in A. Which capacity pays for the read transactions?
choices: Capacity 2, because it's the capacity that stores the data the shortcut points to
Capacity 1, which holds the workspace where the shortcut was created
Neither. Shortcut reads are free
Both, split evenly between the two capacities
questions.explanation: Shortcut transactions count against the capacity of the workspace where the shortcut lives, while the storing capacity pays for storage. A paused source capacity therefore doesn't block downstream consumers' reads. Chargeback models should follow this rule.

questions.question: Do reads and writes to OneLake consume capacity units?
choices: Yes. Reads and writes consume CUs per 10,000 transactions; storage itself is billed per GB
No. All OneLake operations are free once data is stored
Only reads by external engines like Databricks consume CUs
Only writes consume CUs; reads are always free, no matter which engine or shortcut performs them
questions.explanation: OneLake reads cost 104 CU-seconds and writes 1,626 CU-seconds (hot tier) per 10,000 transactions, counted per 4 MB block. Storage is billed per GB without using CUs. From November 15, 2026, some Spark-driven OneLake operations also count toward CU consumption.

questions.question: What happens to OneLake data when its capacity is paused?
choices: Storage is still billed, but transactions against that capacity are rejected
Storage billing stops and the data is archived until the capacity is resumed again
Data is deleted after 24 hours of being paused
Everything keeps working, but at reduced speed
questions.explanation: Pausing stops transactions (so no CUs are consumed) but storage billing continues. Shortcut reads are charged to the consumer's capacity, so downstream consumers on other capacities can still read through shortcuts.

questions.question: How long does OneLake keep soft-deleted files by default, and are they billed?
choices: Soft delete is off by default and must be enabled
One day by default, billed at half the active rate
Seven days by default, billed at the same rate as active data
30 days by default, and soft-deleted data isn't billed during that time
questions.explanation: Soft delete is on by default with 7-day retention, and workspace admins can change it. Soft-deleted data is billed like active data. Deleted workspaces are retained (and billed) for 7 to 90 days.

questions.question: What happens when a customer enables OneLake BCDR on a capacity?
choices: Data replicates asynchronously to the Azure-paired region; storage is billed separately and writes cost more CUs
Data replicates synchronously to any region the admin chooses, at no extra storage or CU cost for the customer
Only Power BI semantic models are replicated; lakehouses are excluded
Fabric guarantees zero data loss and point-in-time consistency after failover
questions.explanation: BCDR is enabled per capacity. The secondary is the Azure-paired region and can't be changed, and replication is asynchronous per file, so failover can lose data and isn't point-in-time consistent. BCDR storage is billed separately, and BCDR writes cost 3,056 CU-seconds per 10,000 versus 1,626 without it.

questions.question: What storage redundancy does OneLake use by default?
choices: Geo-redundant storage across three continents, with automatic failover by Microsoft
Single-disk storage with nightly backups
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) where available, otherwise locally redundant (LRS)
Whatever redundancy the customer's own ADLS account uses
questions.explanation: OneLake uses ZRS where available (at least 12 nines of durability), otherwise LRS (at least 11 nines). Regional disaster recovery needs BCDR, at extra cost.

questions.question: What are the three tabs of the OneLake catalog?
choices: Bronze, Silver and Gold
Ingest, Transform and Serve
Read, Write and Admin
Explore, Govern and Secure
questions.explanation: The OneLake catalog has Explore (discovery, the default tab), Govern (governance health, insights, recommended actions and admin settings) and Secure (a unified view of workspace and OneLake security roles). It's also embedded in Teams, Excel and Copilot Studio.

questions.question: What's the limit on chaining shortcuts that point to other shortcuts?
choices: A maximum of 100 links per chain
Unlimited chaining, as long as all items are in one workspace
A maximum of 5 direct shortcut-to-shortcut links
Shortcuts can't point to other shortcuts at all
questions.explanation: Limits include up to 100,000 shortcuts per item, 100 unique external connections per item, 10 shortcuts per path, and at most 5 chained shortcut links. Names can't contain '%' or '+'. Deep chains are a design smell.

questions.question: A user deletes a file through a shortcut. What happens to the target data?
choices: The deletion is queued for an admin to approve
Nothing happens to the target, because shortcuts are always read-only, whatever the user's permissions
If the user has write permission on the target, the file is deleted at the target too
The file is hidden in the shortcut but kept at the target
questions.explanation: Deleting the shortcut itself leaves the target alone, but deleting files or folders through a shortcut deletes them at the target if the user has write permission there. Treat shortcuts to shared or production data with least-privilege permissions.

questions.question: What extra charge applies when reading OneLake data stored in the cool or cold tier?
choices: Cold data can't be read until it's rehydrated by Microsoft support
No charge at all, because the tier only changes the monthly storage price per GB
A flat $10 per retrieval request
A per-GB retrieval fee in CUs (200 CU-seconds per GB cool, 600 per GB cold)
questions.explanation: Cool and cold tiers lower storage cost but add retrieval fees in CU-seconds per GB (200 cool, 600 cold). Tiering pays off for rarely read data and backfires for data that's queried often.

questions.question: Where can OneLake on-demand billing (preview) be enabled?
choices: On paid capacities (F2 and above) or on F0, where it's on by default
Only on P SKUs
Only on F64 and above
Only on trial capacities, where it replaces the fixed 60-day trial period
questions.explanation: OneLake documents on-demand billing (preview) for operations and storage on paid capacities from F2, and on F0, where it's the default. It's part of Microsoft's 2026 move toward consumption-style Fabric billing alongside provisioned capacity.

questions.question: What does OneLake charge to enforce row-level security on a secured table?
choices: Nothing, because security enforcement is always free in OneLake
A flat F2 capacity reserved for security
1 CU-second per million rows in the secured table
10 Copilot Credits per query
questions.explanation: The consumption page lists OneLake security RLS at 1 CU-second per million rows, and the Table read API at 8 CU-seconds per million rows scanned (billed to the caller). Fine-grained security in Fabric has a small but real compute cost.

questions.question: How is each workspace's OneLake data tied to capacity and region?
choices: Workspaces have no region; OneLake replicates everywhere automatically
Region is chosen per file when data is written
All workspaces share one global region chosen at tenant creation, which can't be changed
Each workspace sits on a capacity, which is tied to a region and billed separately
questions.explanation: The hierarchy is tenant, then workspace, then item. Each workspace is assigned to a capacity in a specific region. Region placement drives data residency, latency and cross-region charges. Fabric data agents, for example, fail if source and agent capacities are in different regions.

questions.question: Which Fabric engines can read data through OneLake shortcuts?
choices: Only Spark notebooks; SQL endpoints and Direct Lake can't follow shortcuts
Spark, SQL analytics endpoints (for Tables), KQL and Power BI Direct Lake
Only the Data Factory copy activity
Only Power BI import models after a refresh
questions.explanation: Shortcuts work across engines: Spark, SQL analytics endpoints (Tables folder), KQL via external tables, and Direct Lake. 'One copy, many engines' is the core value of OneLake. Schema-enabled lakehouses also support schema-level shortcuts.

questions.question: What does Microsoft note about lineage for shortcuts?
choices: Lineage isn't available for any Fabric item
Lineage is complete across every tenant and cloud automatically, including all shortcuts and their external targets too
Shortcuts appear in lineage only after a Purview scan
Lineage shows only same-workspace shortcuts, and shortcuts to warehouses and semantic models have no lineage view
questions.explanation: OneLake lineage has gaps for shortcuts: only same-workspace shortcuts show, and those pointing to warehouses or semantic models have no lineage view. For impact analysis across many workspaces, that's a governance gap to plan around.

questions.question: Data the team needs sits in Amazon S3, and the customer doesn't want to copy it into Fabric. Which feature fits?
choices: A OneLake shortcut to the S3 location
A Dataflow Gen2 that imports the S3 files
A Copy job that runs every five minutes
Open mirroring from S3 into a landing zone
questions.explanation: A shortcut makes data stored elsewhere (S3, ADLS, GCS, Dataverse, other Fabric items) appear in OneLake without copying it. External shortcuts use a cloud connection's credentials, and reads are billed to the capacity of the workspace that holds the shortcut.

questions.question: What's the difference between a OneLake shortcut and database mirroring?
choices: A shortcut works only for Fabric items; mirroring works only for files in Amazon S3 and Google Cloud
A shortcut copies data into OneLake on a schedule; mirroring points at the data without copying it
A shortcut points at data where it already is; database mirroring replicates the data into OneLake
They're the same feature: 'mirroring' is the name used when a shortcut points at a database
questions.explanation: Shortcuts make data stored elsewhere appear in OneLake without copying it. Database mirroring replicates a source database into OneLake as Delta tables in near real time. Azure Databricks mirroring is the exception that blurs the line: it mirrors metadata and reads the Delta files through shortcuts.

questions.question: A user queries one table through an internal shortcut to another Fabric lakehouse and another through a shortcut to Amazon S3. Whose credentials read each?
choices: Both use the user's identity, because OneLake passes it through to every target
The internal shortcut uses the connection's credentials; the S3 shortcut uses the user's
The internal shortcut uses the user's identity; the S3 shortcut uses the cloud connection's credentials
Both use the workspace identity, because shortcuts never use a person's identity
questions.explanation: Internal shortcuts check the caller's identity against the target. External shortcuts, such as S3 or ADLS, use the credentials stored in the cloud connection, so anyone who can read the shortcut can read what that connection can. Reads are billed to the capacity of the workspace holding the shortcut.

questions.question: Before turning on OneLake BCDR for a capacity, what should the customer accept?
choices: That every workspace becomes read-only until the team runs its first failover drill
Extra storage charges, costlier writes, and possible data loss in a failover
A move to a P SKU, because BCDR isn't available on F SKUs
That BCDR doubles the capacity's CUs at no extra charge
questions.explanation: OneLake BCDR replicates data asynchronously to the Azure-paired region. It adds separate storage charges and makes writes cost more, and because replication is asynchronous, a failover can lose recent data. Treat it as a business decision with clear recovery objectives.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: What are Fabric's three types of mirroring?
choices: Azure mirroring, AWS mirroring and on-premises mirroring, based on source location
Full, incremental and snapshot mirroring, chosen per table depending on how often its source data changes
Hot mirroring, cool mirroring and cold mirroring, based on storage tier
Database mirroring (copies data), metadata mirroring (shortcuts) and open mirroring (apps push changes)
questions.explanation: Database mirroring replicates databases into Delta tables; metadata mirroring (Azure Databricks, Dremio) syncs metadata and reads data through shortcuts; open mirroring lets any app write change data into a landing zone. The type determines what's copied, what's free and how fresh the data is.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: Which mirroring type does Fabric use for Azure Databricks?
choices: Metadata mirroring. Catalog structure syncs and data is read through shortcuts
There's no mirroring for Azure Databricks; it requires pipelines
Open mirroring. Databricks must push changes through APIs
Database mirroring. Every Delta table is copied into OneLake on a fixed schedule
questions.explanation: Azure Databricks uses metadata mirroring: only the catalog structure is mirrored, and data is read in place through shortcuts. Snowflake supports database and metadata mirroring, and Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SAP, SQL Server and BigQuery use database mirroring.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: What does Fabric charge for the compute that replicates data into a mirrored database?
choices: Replication compute is billed at 3x the normal CU rate
It consumes the source database's Fabric capacity at the standard rate
Nothing. Replication compute is free and doesn't consume capacity
It's billed in Copilot Credits
questions.explanation: Background replication compute is free. Storage is free up to 1 TB per CU. Querying mirrored data (SQL, Power BI, Spark) consumes CUs normally. Source-side costs, such as change-feed load on the source database, aren't covered by Fabric.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: When is mirrored data billed as regular OneLake storage?
choices: Only when the source is outside Azure
Never. Mirrored storage is free without any limit, whatever the capacity size
When it exceeds the free mirroring allowance, or while the capacity is paused
Only during the first 30 days after mirroring starts
questions.explanation: Microsoft: you pay for OneLake storage if you exceed the free mirroring limit or when the capacity is paused. A running capacity is also required for replication, and pausing stops it. 'Pause at night to save money' breaks near-real-time mirroring.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: How fresh can database-mirrored data be, according to Microsoft?
choices: Guaranteed under one second with a financially backed SLA
Only when an admin manually triggers a sync
Changes can be published as fast as every 15 seconds, depending on volume, region and network
Exactly once every 24 hours on a fixed schedule, regardless of how much the source data changes
questions.explanation: Database mirroring is near real-time: changes can publish as often as every 15 seconds, but there's no numeric SLA and latency depends on change volume, region, network and gateway compute. Set expectations carefully for operational reporting.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: What is open mirroring?
choices: A way to mirror Fabric data out to Snowflake and Databricks
Any application or partner writes change files into a OneLake landing zone, and Fabric merges them into Delta tables
A free Microsoft service that mirrors any SaaS application automatically, with no code or partner involvement needed
Mirroring that makes Fabric data publicly readable on the internet
questions.explanation: Open mirroring gives you a landing-zone URL. Your app or an ecosystem partner writes files in the landing-zone format, and Fabric merges inserts, updates and deletes into Delta tables with a read-only SQL analytics endpoint. It extends mirroring to sources Microsoft doesn't support natively.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: How does Direct Lake differ from Import mode in Power BI?
choices: It copies the full data into the model on each scheduled refresh
It caches report images rather than data
It queries the source database live for every visual, exactly like DirectQuery, with no in-memory caching at all
It reads Delta tables in OneLake directly, loading columns into memory on demand rather than importing a copy
questions.explanation: Direct Lake avoids import copies: a 'refresh' (framing) only updates metadata pointers to the latest Parquet files, and columns are paged into memory when a query first needs them. It combines import-like speed with freshness, within guardrails.

questions.sectionName: Mirroring, Direct Lake and Power BI
questions.question: What is 'framing' in Direct Lake?
choices: A report feature that freezes a visual's layout
A refresh that copies only metadata, pointing the model at the latest Delta Parquet files
A refresh that re-imports every row into the VertiPaq engine, just like an Import model
Partitioning a model into date ranges for incremental refresh
